item.title: Intense and Gifted People Struggle in Therapy
item.description:
Intelligence

Intense and Gifted People Struggle in Therapy

When high IQ, highly sensitive, and emotionally intense people seek therapy.

Posted July 22, 2026

Key points
  • Gifted and emotionally deep adults often leave therapy feeling more alone than when they arrived.
  • Many gifted clients end up managing and protecting the therapist's feelings in sessions.
  • A good therapist does not need to match your speed; you want them to be honest when they miss something.
  • Learning to accept a "good enough" therapist, rather than a perfect one, is a part of the work.

Gifted and intellectually intense adults frequently report dissatisfaction with conventional therapy. Many describe leaving sessions feeling more alone than when they arrived, and more convinced than ever that no one can receive their full, true self and meet them where they are.

The pattern often begins long before the therapy room. If you are gifted and highly empathic, you have probably spent the majority of your life solving your own problems. From childhood, life has been about being there for others. You read the room before anyone else did, absorbed the tension, looked after the emotional needs of the people who were supposed to be looking after yours. Friends lean on your clarity and your patience, and you give willingly. And when you try to reverse that dynamic, when you look for someone to lean on, you often hit a wall. You get told you think too much, worry too much. Or worse, they simply quietly withdraw. After enough of these experiences, you stopped trying.

Reluctantly, often with little hope, and usually as a last resort, you decide to talk to a therapist.

What Happens When You Finally Seek Help

With all that you have introspected and read and researched, you likely arrive already armed with a thorough understanding of your own history and psychology. You are fluent, eloquent, and to most observers you come across as psychologically minded and full of insights. You deliver your history with such clarity and fluency that most therapists do not challenge it. The session appears to be progressing.

But when you walk out, something feels off. You feel missed. Something is lacking. Your heart has a mild sinking feeling, and the time you just spent feels somewhat empty. The therapist seemed slow, or maybe not slow exactly, but something was not landing. There was just a blatant gap between what you were saying and what the person across from you was receiving. Was it you who needed to be more patient? Or was this genuinely just a bad match? You were not sure.

Sometimes, when you persevere with having sessions even when it does not feel right, something worse begins to happen. You begin to notice that you are doing more work than the therapist. You sense when the therapist is straining to follow, and you default to adjusting yourself to help them out. You edit yourself, slow down, reword things, and soften a difficult disclosure when you sense it will overwhelm the room. In the end, you find yourself back at the very dynamic you were trying to escape from: being the person who needs to manage everyone's emotions or shield them from your full self.

Why You Stay Even When It Is Not Working

When a highly sensitive or gifted adult decides to reach out, the unnamed longing underneath is likely a deep and painful one: the longing for someone who is genuinely strong enough to be the "bigger" figure who can hold them so they are not the one holding everything together, as they have always done. What keeps you in a therapy that is not working might be the unconscious longing to experience the therapist as a calm, powerful, and wise parental figure who can provide what was missed in childhood. Understandably, when you finally find someone who might be that person, your attachment needs are powerfully activated. And so you stay, and you try, and you keep trying to make it work. But if it truly is not the right person, perseverance alone will not fix it, and staying can deepen the wound it was supposed to heal.

The truth is, you are not beyond help, and you are not without needs. Your moral sensitivity can be so fierce that you hold yourself to standards no one asked for. Your perfectionism can get so loud that it drowns out everything else, and when emotions hit at that intensity, words stop working. Yes, you do a lot of your own research and processing, but sometimes your mind gets so chaotic you do not even know what you want. You can describe your pain with extraordinary clarity and still not be changed by the description. Understanding why you are stuck and actually becoming unstuck are different processes.

The Therapist You Want

Ideally, you want a therapist who can meet your intensity directly, without shrinking from it or pathologising it. They need to not get defensive when you correct them, because you will correct them, plainly and with a straight face, and with most people that can be received as an attack. They do not need to keep up with your full speed. But you want someone who is secure enough to tell you honestly when they have missed something, rather than nodding along and pretending they followed.

A working dynamic has two elements: warmth and challenge, and something about the dynamic doesn't quite work when the therapist leans too heavily on one at the expense of the other. Warmth without challenge becomes a cosy room where nothing changes. Challenge without warmth becomes another environment where you feel you are being assessed. The best fit is someone who can do both: who can sit with you in genuine empathy and also push you past the polished version of your story into the material underneath it.

You may also be a fast-moving person who hates stagnation. Patience is something worth practising, and mindfulness can be extremely useful, but you also need to feel that you have a genuine partner in the work, someone who is actively invested in creating change with you, not just sitting across from you while you figure it out alone again.

Moving Forward

If the dynamic with a therapist feels wrong, it is not a moral failing to leave. You are not your therapist’s therapist, and it is not your job to protect your therapist's feelings.

But trusting your gut does not mean chasing perfection. No therapist will match you completely, and waiting for one who does is another way the longing keeps you stuck. The desire for the perfect therapist, the one who finally gets you completely, is often the old wound talking. Winnicott wrote that good enough parenting is good enough, and the same principle applies here. Learning to live with good enough, in your therapist and in yourself, is actually part of the work. It is part of growing up, of maturing, of becoming a person who can tolerate imperfect love and be thoroughly nourished by it.

You are not too much. You are not beyond help. You are a person with a specific kind of mind and a specific kind of need, and both of those deserve to be met with honesty, warmth, and courage. The right container is likely out there waiting for you, and it is good enough, though not perfect. The therapist that is right for you will sometimes miss things and sometimes be slower than you. But they will stay in the room with you.

And that is still worth pursuing and staying for.

item.title: The Planetary Health Diet May Save Your Brain and the Earth
item.description:
Diet

The Planetary Health Diet May Save Your Brain and the Earth

The modern diet accelerates brain aging and increases global climate change.

Posted July 22, 2026

Key points
  • Brain disorders are the leading cause of illness and disability, affecting a third of the world’s population.
  • The world’s consumption of animal products significantly contributes to pollution and global climate change.
  • Healthy dietary choices and less animal consumption can improve brain health while slowing climate change.

Brain disorders are now the leading cause of illness and disability, affecting over one-third of the world’s population. As the population continues to grow and age, this burden is expected to further increase in the coming decades. Therefore, brain health has become a global priority. Healthy dietary change is now recognized as a key strategy to improve population health since poor diet is a major contributor to the global burden of disease.

Healthy dietary choices, especially eating much less animal products, would also contribute greatly to environmental sustainability and climate change mitigation. The world’s consumption of animal products significantly contributes to environmental pollution through methane emissions, water contamination, and land degradation, making cattle farming a major ecological concern. Cows are major producers of methane, a potent greenhouse gas approximately 23 to 28 times more effective than carbon dioxide at trapping heat over a century. Globally, given that there are over 1.5 billion cows, 1.3 billion sheep, 14 billion chickens, and 1 billion pigs worldwide, livestock accounts for about 20 percent of greenhouse gas emissions, with cattle contributing the majority. Their manure contaminates rivers and streams with pathogens and organic matter, leading to algal blooms, oxygen depletion, and the death of aquatic life. Cattle farming also drives deforestation, particularly in regions like the Amazon, to create pastureland or grow feed crops such as soybeans.

Therefore, one potential path to reduce the impact of global climate change involves a significant change in the human diet. In 2019, the EAT–Lancet Commission (a collaboration between a science-based global platform for food system transformation and The Lancet, a leading medical journal) proposed the Planetary Health Diet to promote both human and environmental health (Willett and team, 2019). This diet mainly consists of plant-rich foods, such as whole grains, fruits, and vegetables, and only small amounts of animal-based foods.

Previous studies have shown that adherence to the Planetary Health Diet resulted in a decreased risk of cardiovascular disease, hypertension, asthma, and mortality. A recent study investigated whether the Planetary Health Diet also benefits brain health. The authors (Li and team, 2026) examined a large dataset from the UK Biobank (Sudlow and team, 2015) to determine the relationship between the Planetary Health Diet and brain disorder risk.

They reported that the highest adherence to the Planetary Health Diet was associated with a 12%, 13 %, 13 %, and 19 % lower risk of stroke, depression, anxiety, and multimorbidity, respectively, and had a significant role in decelerating biological aging. Their analyses discovered an inverse relationship between the Planetary Health Diet and these common brain disorders. The link between the Planetary Health Diet and brain disorder risk was more pronounced in adult males under 65 years of age. The mechanistic reasons why compliance with the Planetary Health Diet lowers brain disorder risk are not fully understood; however, this diet shares many features of the Mediterranean diet that are also associated with prevention of cardiovascular disease and cognitive aging. The dietary components of both diets are rich in antioxidants and polyphenols that have the potential to inhibit neuroinflammation in relation to brain disorders and attenuate neuroinflammation via indirect immune pathways from the gut microbiome and systemic circulation [to read more about this topic, see: Your Brain on Food].

There are, however, some important caveats that should be considered. The authors estimate that over one billion people worldwide may not be able to afford the EAT–Lancet diet (Springmann and team,2021), and iron and zinc inadequacies and deficiencies are common among individuals with high consumption of plant-rich foods (Beal and team, 2023). However, these findings provide convincing evidence that it is possible to reduce brain disorder risk, slow down age-related decline, and advance food system sustainability to reduce global climate change.

item.title: Three Insights Into Gaslighting at Work
item.description:
Gaslighting

Three Insights Into Gaslighting at Work

Learn strategies to identify manipulation if you're being maltreated at work.

Posted July 22, 2026

Key points
  • Examining workplace abuse through a strengths-based lens helps expose gaslighting.
  • Workplaces may focus on targets' mental weakness when the focus should be on perpetrators' dysfunction.
  • To maintain mental strength, remain clearsighted about the unjust harm being done to you.

When we examine workplace bullying in an extreme form, namely the punitive treatment of LGBT military personnel over the decades, targets of less systemic workplace abuse can gain valuable insights. In this post, the insights in the military examples are juxtaposed with four non-military, bullying workplaces described in The Gaslit Brain, in order to help targeted employees to identify when gaslighting is being used.

Instead of the more typical pathologizing of LGBT military personnel, Dr. Heliana Ramirez and Dr. Paul Sterzing, social work experts and researchers, focus on the “strength, resilience, and resistance” demonstrated by targeted service members and veterans. Valuable insights can be gained by their approach for all targets and survivors of systemic workplace bullying.

Gaslighting used in workplace abuse

The first insight emerges from examining the way perpetrators use gaslighting to fault those they target for maltreatment. Citing extensive research, Ramirez and Sterzing reveal “centuries of official and unofficial anti-LGBT military policies” that positioned victims as the ones doing wrong, being mentally ill, and unfit for work.

The textbook reversal of the bullying offender and the targeted victim has been normalized and systematized in the military. The gaslighting is clear in that the discriminatory, un-empathic, callous treatment of victims is justified by perpetrators who position their targets as mentally ill, morally corrupt, or mentally deficient.

Neuroscientific research documented in The Gaslit Brain provides evidence for mental illness residing in perpetrators of abuse, not the victims they target. Those who harm others in the workplace frequently have brain deficiencies and injuries that are visible on brain scans. The science reveals that not only are discriminatory, unempathic, callous individuals unfit for duty because of their mental dysfunction, but they are often outright destructive and dangerous.

Making the contributions of targets disappear

The second insight that emerges from Ramirez and Sterzing’s research centres on decades of erasing the “contributions” of targeted LGBT service members. Analyzing four non-military workplaces, The Gaslit Brain reveals this same pattern. Individuals put in the out-group for having too much talent, acting on too much integrity, having the courage to speak up about wrong-doing, all resulted in the erasure of their contributions to the workplace.

If LGBT service members, or the targets of bullying in The Gaslit Brain, were indeed causing workplace issues, problems, crises of one kind or another, their track records should be under scrutiny, not made to vanish. Their track records should provide a history of wrong-doing or weakness that justifies termination. What we find documented in Ramirez and Sterzing’s research is the opposite, and the same insight is seen in The Gaslit Brain. The contributions of targets are, in fact, valuable. In an abusive workplace, they must be erased as they risk exposing the gaslighting at work.

If you are being maltreated and gaslit, instead of your track record providing the evidence for an unfortunate work history, it will instead be erased. It is a red flag of maltreatment and manipulation. When you are being targeted, and a false narrative is being constructed around you, it’s hard to stay clear-sighted about the moral injustice that is occurring.

Maltreatment causes mental instability and suffering

The third insight comes from Ramirez and Sterzing recording the way LGBT service members were “banished through early discharges” or institutionalized in psychiatric facilities. In the case studies of The Gaslit Brain, a lesser version occurred whereby the targets of bullying and abuse left the workplace through constructive dismissal and sought out mental health counselling. Even beyond the oppressive military workplace, being targeted can lead to the loss of one’s position, livelihood, and a need for mental health support. You can see the way targets are gaslit into thinking their psychological suffering requires healing and repair, especially when they are not commended for their incredible courage and mental strength to resist intensive abuse.

Whether being discharged or escaping the workplace abuse to save one’s health, targets can be left with a sense that they are the ones who are weak, unwell, or unstable, even though the kind of abuse they endured is well-documented in research to cause extreme mental distress. The great power of the abusive workplace is to terminate an employee. But Ramirez and Sterzing provide targets with a way to understand the injustice and wastefulness of their maltreatment.

How to resist the gaslighting and see clearly

Source: Clarence Alford / Pixabay

Ramirez and Sterzing provide a final hard-hitting exposure of the gaslighting that surrounds the military's maltreatment of sexual minority service members: “The costs of these anti-LGBT military policies are profound, with the U.S. military spending $193.3 million from 2004 to 2009 to train and replace LGBT military personnel” who had been discharged. In other words, the targets were contributing effectively. They were valuable and they were costly to replace. If they lacked contributions, had poor track records, were mentally weak or unstable, it should not have been so massively expensive to replace them.

Likewise, as outlined in The Gaslit Brain, it would have been costly to replace an award-winning teacher with a PhD, a top-tier Nike executive, a highly-promoted counter-terrorism expert, and an award-winning law professor, but all those workplaces chose to remove their talent and replace them at great cost. This final insight can help those targeted for workplace discrimination or abuse to see clearly that the way they are being spoken of, treated, and positioned is false.

Workplaces that have systemic abuse issues can make targets feel as if the discharge, firing, or constructive dismissal is their own fault and lead them to believe it’s due to their mental weakness. Ramirez and Sterzing’s research shows that not only are workers being bullied out of their positions and careers, they are being grossly misled to believe the problem lies with them. Their insights expose the gaslighting and show how great the abuse was that they endured.

Ramirez and Sterzing’s approach is strengths-based and commends the remarkable resilience and fortitude of the targets. Their work acts as a reminder that not only has appalling harm been done to targets by perpetrators, but these perpetrators use gaslighting to further abuse and manipulate. Most importantly, while perpetrators rarely if ever recover from the brain dysfunctions that make them harm others, targets – as shown by Ramirez and Sterzing – can recover effectively and repair the moral injuries done to them.

item.title: Canaries in the Marketplace and What It Means to Be Human
item.description:
Genetics

Canaries in the Marketplace and What It Means to Be Human

How markets reshape desire, and what we risk losing in the genomic age.

Posted July 22, 2026

Key points
  • Markets satisfy our appetites, but they also reshape them.
  • Freedom of choice does not answer whether our desires are worth cultivating.
  • Cultural norms can shift gradually until what once seemed troubling feels normal.
  • Sandel's warning: Mastery over nature may change how we see our children and each other.

If we view the market strictly through the lens of individual freedom, it is difficult to make a case against fast food or modern sexual culture. Neither was imposed on an unwilling public. Both succeeded because they responded to genuine human desires, and competition made satisfying those desires easier, cheaper, and more profitable than ever before.

Yet no one set out to create an obesity and metabolic disease crisis. Nor did anyone intend to create a culture marked by rising loneliness, declining intimacy, and dissatisfaction with relationships. In both cases, millions of voluntary choices accumulated into outcomes that few people, across political or religious divides, would regard as a success.

Markets are remarkably good at giving people what they want. They are less equipped to ask whether every desire they satisfy contributes to human flourishing. As market principles permeate more areas of life, moral legitimacy increasingly rests on a single question: Did you consent? Yet that question neglects a deeper one: Was the desire to which you consented worth cultivating?

Source: Unknown Author / Wikimedia Commons

The French sociologist Émile Durkheim used the concept of anomie to describe a condition in which traditional moral frameworks weakened, leaving appetites without clear direction or restraint. He worried that rapid industrialization, combined with the decline of religious and local community attachments, had weakened society’s ability to regulate desire. Freed from older constraints, individuals could become vulnerable to endless striving and dissatisfaction.

Viewed through a Durkheimian lens, many features of contemporary life echo the concerns he raised. We possess unprecedented freedom of choice, but choice alone cannot tell us which desires build healthier lives and communities.

The lesson is not that markets are inherently harmful. They have generated extraordinary prosperity and improved countless aspects of human life. Rather, market freedom must be considered alongside the consequences of allowing powerful institutions to cultivate appetites without meaningful limits.

Commercial Incentives Change Consumption Habits

Consider soda. Decades ago, soft drinks were closer to dessert than a daily staple—a small indulgence rather than an ordinary part of every meal. Through commercial incentives, aggressive marketing, and the engineering of “bliss points,” routine consumption gradually became normalized. No single company or consumer decision created today’s health problems. They emerged through countless choices that seemed reasonable in isolation.

A similar process has unfolded in our sexual culture. Over the past several decades, sexual imagery has become increasingly integrated into commercial life. Advertising, entertainment, social media, and online pornography have each contributed to a gradual recalibration of what feels normal. The transformation did not arrive through a single dramatic moment, but through thousands of small shifts.

In both cases, markets did what markets do: they responded to demand. The question is whether satisfying a desire can ever be decoupled from the cultivation of character.

Durkheim’s conception of human nature helps illuminate this tension. Human beings, he argued, are homo duplex—two-level beings divided between individual and social impulses. We possess desires rooted in our biological inheritance: pleasure, security, status, and recognition. Yet we also have capacities shaped by social life: discipline, commitment, obligation, and self-sacrifice.

Markets are exceptionally effective at appealing to our first set of impulses. They are less effective at cultivating the second. Their incentives naturally reward consumption, novelty, and immediate satisfaction. The result is that protective norms can gradually erode before we recognize their value. We hardly notice until the cultural ground has shifted beneath us.

The question, then, is what happens when this same market logic is applied not merely to what we consume, but to who we become.

The Genomic Marketplace

Fast food and modern sexual culture are canaries in the marketplace. They reveal what can happen when powerful industries become extraordinarily effective at stimulating human appetites, while lacking any inherent mechanism that ensures those appetites ultimately serve us well.

Source: Gemini AI image

If markets have transformed what we consume and how we understand intimacy, genetic technologies may transform what we expect human beings themselves to become.

This is the concern at the heart of Michael Sandel’s critique of enhancement. His worry is not solely that genetic technologies may be misused or increase inequality. Rather, he asks what happens when more dimensions of human life become objects of design and optimization.

The issue is not whether parents should want healthy, flourishing children—they obviously should. The question is whether the pursuit of mastery gradually displaces older virtues such as humility, acceptance, and what Sandel calls openness to the unbidden.

A culture that increasingly sees every limitation as a problem to be solved may slowly lose the ability to receive imperfect human beings as gifts rather than achievements. The deeper concern is not only what technologies allow us to do. It is how quickly expectations may change once those technologies become available.

Behavioral genetics suggests that many traits with profound consequences for human lives—including cognitive ability, personality, and vulnerability to psychological disorders—are influenced by genetic variation. At present, there is broad agreement around using genetic screening to prevent serious disease. The harder question is whether that same logic will gradually expand from treating illness to selecting embryos for increasingly broader traits.

As scientific possibilities expand and market incentives develop, practices that once seemed extraordinary may eventually appear not only acceptable, but expected.

Sandel’s warning, then, is not that we will suddenly stop loving our children. It is that we may gradually come to love them differently.

Just as markets have quietly reshaped our relationships with food and sexuality, they may eventually reshape our aspirations for the next generation. The danger is not that this transformation will arrive through a dramatic rupture. It is that we may accept it gradually—one small adjustment at a time—until what was once a protective boundary becomes simply another matter of personal preference.

The tragedy is that we may not recognize what has been lost until a future generation inherits the consequences of choices that once appeared to represent nothing more than freedom.
